newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - NZ Business weeklies - Feb 14.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - NZ Business weeklies - Feb 14.

text.p: The competence and management style of Serious Fraud Office director Chas Sturt were called into question on Thursday by the SFO's former chief prosecutor, Susan Pilgrim. Also revealed in Pilgrim's evidence to the winebox Commission of Inquiry was corroboration of an issue raised in The Independent on 16 February last year -- that Sturt and his office failed to investigate key winebox deals before telling parliament in late March 1994 that there was no evidence of serious or complex fraud. Sturt, said Pilgrim, did not give the impression of "having an intimate, working knowledge of financial transactions". Page 1.

Air Nauru chief executive Rex Banks is threatening to sue Civil Aviation Authority director Kevin Ward personally for NZ$1.5 million. Banks threatened legal action against the CAA in December when, at the last minute, it declined Air Nauru's application to land its Boeing 737-400 here. Now he has his sights set firmly on Ward alone. Banks says he is coming to New Zealand on 24 February and hopes to serve the legal documents on Ward himself. Page 1.

Aotearoa Radio is considering shutting down operations following reductions in funding by Maori broadcasting agency Te Mangai Paho. And a second Maori broadcaster -- Mana Maori News -- is considering its options after it reached stalemate in its funding negotiations. Trustees of national radio network Aotearoa Maori Radio (no relation to the beleaguered television station of the same name) are deciding today (Friday) whether they will close the station to avoid personal financial liability following a 60 percent cut in funding from Te Mangai Paho. Page 1.

An exemption to the Commerce Act, allowing international airlines to engage in government-approved price-fixing, has raised the hackles of the Commerce Commission. The commission says it is unable to investigate a three percent international fare rise because the increase was authorised by the Transport Ministry following a recommendation from international airline industry group IATA. Page 2.

An historic open-skies aviation agreement with Singapore looks likely to go ahead this year after Treasurer and Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters this week came out with a firm endorsement of the former government's open skies policy. In a state of the nation address in Wellington on Tuesday, Peters told business leaders "the government remains committed to reciprocal liberalisation where possible, and we are keen to pursue bilateral open skies agreements in the Asia-Pacific and beyond." Page 3.

Cabinet has given TVNZ the go-ahead to increase its shareholding in pay-tv operator Sky Television. TVNZ owns 16.4 percent of Sky but wants to expand this, believing a strong foothold in pay-tv is crucial to its future. Informed sources suggest the network wants to lift its stake between 25 and 33 percent. The exact percentage approved by Cabinet is not known. TVNZ is now awaiting advice on whether the expansion would cause problems with the Commerce Commission. Page 3.

Wang New Zealand is considering acquiring other computer services companies, including some across the Tasman. The company may change its name later this year, cutting its last national tie with United States company, Wang Laboratories. Office supplies group Blue Star, currently owning 88.6 percent of shares in Wang NZ, has an option to acquire the 9.8 percent share held by Wang Labs. This will take Blue Star past the 90 percent shareholding threshold where it can compulsorily acquire the remaining 1.6 percent belonging to minor interests. Page 4.

Homeowners living near the Devonport Naval Base face plummeting property values as the Navy plans to recommission tunnels connecting huge fuel storage tanks buried beneath their homes. Few residents knew of the underground fuel facility when they bought their homes. The Navy wants to recommission the tunnels behind the base because of costly fuel contamination problems associated with its current storage facilities. Page 4.

Power New Zealand this week had its hand slapped by the Advertising Standards Complaints Board (ASCB) over newspaper advertisements it ran in the Te Awamutu Courier and Waihi Leader last October slamming the Waipa District Council for selling its Power NZ shares to Mercury Energy. The Waipa District Council complained the advertisements breached the advertising code of ethics and rules about truthful presentation, denigration and advocacy advertising. The ASCB upheld the complaint. Page 7.

The Commerce Ministry rejects oil industry suggestions its tracking of petrol price margins is flawed. Oil industry spokesmen were reacting to Energy Minister Max Bradford suggestions that the four main oil companies are inflating the retail price of petrol. Bradford this week produced Commerce Ministry data showing the margin between the international benchmark (Singapore's export price) and the New Zealand retail price has increased from 15 cents in 1990 to 22.5 cents in the third quarter of 1996. Page 7.

A demand for relief from levy payments was Federated Farmers' response to the Meat Board's $3.4 million profit in 1995/96. The board should be "ashamed" of a profit of that magnitude, reaped in a year when sheep and beef farmers were battling low commodity prices and a high Kiwi dollar, said meat and wool section chairman Edward Orr. On top of $70 million built up in reserves, the profit was "obscene". Page 7.
